title: Make It Stick
hook: The calendar does what inspiration cannot: it makes memory come back after the room has changed.
counterintuition: Most people assume the favorite trick is the shortcut. The twist is that learning lasts better when small methods are scheduled to catch one another's misses.
tryThisNow: Choose one skill and schedule three short returns this week: one recall, one mixed practice, and one repair check after feedback.
keyTakeaway: Make learning stick by building a repeatable cycle: retrieve, space, mix, check, repair, and repeat until the skill can return under changed conditions.

breakdown.fastRead:
Clio writes four boxes on a pharmacy receipt at 7:06 p.m. in the campus cafe: recall, mix, check, repair. Her exam is Friday. A cram block would feel dramatic. The receipt looks dull. It is also a system.

One method helps. A routine helps more. Retrieval makes memory produce. Spacing makes it return. Interleaving trains choice. Calibration checks confidence. Repair fixes the miss. Put the moves on a calendar and the learning has a place to come back.
breakdown.deepRead:
Clio writes four boxes on a pharmacy receipt at 7:06 p.m. in the campus cafe. Recall, mix, check, repair. Her exam is Friday, and a single cram block keeps calling to her because it feels heroic. The receipt is less heroic. It gives Tuesday to recall, Wednesday to mixed problems, Thursday to a no-cue check and repair.

This is the synthesis. Each method does a different job. Retrieval pulls the idea back. Spacing asks it to return after time. Interleaving makes the learner choose among near neighbors. Calibration tests confidence against performance. Repair turns misses into the next round.

Gareth sees why the pieces need one another at 4:55 p.m. in the maintenance shop. His old training tips faded because they lived on posters. The new routine puts a five-minute recall at shift start, one mixed fault card after lunch, and a repair log before clock-out. Nothing is flashy. More faults get fixed without help.

Do not collect tactics like souvenirs. Build a cycle small enough to run. The methods stick when they have a schedule, a trigger, and a repair path.

The calendar gives memory a place to come back.

Saskia proves the point two weeks later in the staff hall. Her friend remembers the drama of the six-hour cram, but not the code-card sequence. Saskia's weekly cycle feels dull while it runs. It is less dull when the surprise drill arrives and the steps come back.
breakdown.fullRead:
Clio writes four boxes on a pharmacy receipt at 7:06 p.m. in the campus cafe. The espresso grinder screams behind the counter. Her exam is Friday. A cram block would feel serious, almost brave. The receipt looks plain: recall Tuesday, mixed problems Wednesday, no-cue check Thursday, repair before bed.

That plain receipt is the final move. Durable learning is not one favorite trick. It is a cycle. Retrieval makes memory produce instead of recognize. Spacing makes the idea return after some forgetting. Interleaving forces choice among similar cases. Calibration asks whether confidence matches performance. Repair takes the miss and builds the next attempt around it.

Gareth sees the difference at 4:55 p.m. in the maintenance shop. Last year he taped training tips above the tool crib. People liked them. Two weeks later, the same faults came back. This year he builds a routine: Monday recall of shutdown steps, Wednesday mixed fault cards, Friday repair log with one retest. The wall looks less inspiring. The machines go down less often for the same mistakes.

A single tactic can fail by being lonely. Retrieval without spacing can become a one-day burst. Spacing without retrieval can become vague good intention. Interleaving without feedback can leave confusion in place. Calibration without repair can make people accurate about weakness but no stronger. The cycle matters because each move catches what another move misses.

Paloma says it plainly at 8:22 a.m. while planning a certification group with Wen. One favorite method is a tool. The weekly routine is the bench, the light, and the habit of picking the tool up again.

Keep the system small. A giant plan dies when the week gets busy. A ten-minute recall, a short mixed set, and one repair note can survive. The point is not to admire learning science. The point is to give memory repeated work under slightly changed conditions until it can return when needed.

The calendar does what inspiration cannot: it makes memory come back after the room has changed.

Saskia proves the point two weeks later in the staff hall. Her friend remembers the drama of the six-hour cram, but not the code-card sequence. Saskia's weekly cycle felt dull while it ran: Tuesday recall, Thursday scenarios, Saturday repair. It is less dull when the surprise drill arrives and the steps come back after the test room is gone.

Thabo adds the missing piece in a restaurant kitchen. His apprentices already practice knife cuts, sauces, and plating. The same errors still return on Fridays. He clips a repair ticket to the station: what missed, when to retry, what changed. The system does not merely find errors. It schedules their return.

Inga makes the personal version on her apartment floor. A list of tips becomes two calendar blocks. Tuesday recall. Friday mixed practice and repair. The advice loses shine when it becomes an alarm, but it gains a future.

A learning system should be small enough to run and complete enough to catch the common failures. If it cannot fit on a normal week, it will not survive. If it never checks or repairs, it will only admire itself.

examples.title: Clio writes the learning cycle on a receipt

planSpec.audience: students tempted by a single cram block
planSpec.stakes: whether methods become a runnable weekly system
planSpec.requiredBeat: she builds an exam week system instead of a cram block

examples.scenario: Clio writes four boxes on a pharmacy receipt at 7:06 p.m. in the campus cafe, espresso grounds stuck to the heel of her hand. Her pharmacology exam is Friday. The tempting plan is one long Thursday cram with every slide open. The receipt plan is quieter: Tuesday recall, Wednesday mixed cases, Thursday no-cue check, Thursday night repair. She folds the receipt once and has to decide which plan gets the calendar alert.
examples.whatToDo: Put the four-box cycle on the calendar and keep each block short: retrieve, mix, check, repair. Let review support the cycle, not replace it.
examples.whyItMatters: The cram block leans on intensity. The cycle makes memory return, choose, and repair across time, which is what the exam will demand.

examples.title: Gareth takes the tips off the tool-crib wall

planSpec.audience: managers whose advice fades after posters
planSpec.stakes: whether recurring practice changes shop behavior
planSpec.requiredBeat: he reviews a training routine that faded

examples.scenario: Gareth stands by the tool crib at 4:55 p.m., peeling last year's laminated training tip from the cinderblock wall. The tip was popular. The same shutdown errors returned in two weeks. His new sheet is uglier: Monday recall at shift start, Wednesday mixed fault cards, Friday repair log and retest. He looks at the blank wall where the poster was and has to decide whether workers need another reminder or a routine that keeps calling the skill back.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the poster with scheduled practice: brief recall, mixed fault choice, and a repair log with a retest for the missed step.
examples.whyItMatters: Advice fades when it has no return path. A routine makes the skill show up again after time, variation, and feedback.

examples.title: Paloma asks Wen what the favorite tactic misses

planSpec.audience: learners attached to one favorite method
planSpec.stakes: whether the group covers different failure modes
planSpec.requiredBeat: they debate one favorite tactic versus a full cycle

examples.scenario: Paloma caps a black marker at 8:22 a.m. in the union hall, bagels cooling beside a stack of certification handouts. "Flashcards are enough," Wen says. Paloma points at the whiteboard columns: recall, spacing, mixed cases, check, repair. "Flashcards help recall. What handles choosing the right case? What handles overconfidence?" Wen tears a bagel in half and looks at the board. "So my tool is good, but it is not the whole bench."
examples.whatToDo: Keep the flashcards, then add spacing, mixed cases, no-cue checks, and repair rounds. Give each method a job in the weekly cycle.
examples.whyItMatters: One tactic catches one weakness. The full cycle catches several: forgetting, poor selection, false confidence, and unrepaired gaps.

examples.title: Saskia watches the quiet weekly plan beat the burst

planSpec.stakes: whether a weekly routine beats a dramatic cram
planSpec.requiredBeat: she predicts the weekly system will beat the burst

examples.scenario: Saskia tapes a recertification checklist above her locker at 6:18 a.m., sanitizer smell sharp in the staff hall. She predicts her quiet weekly plan will beat her usual Sunday burst: Tuesday recall, Thursday mixed scenarios, Saturday repair. Her friend laughs and studies for six hours the night before. On test day, the burst feels fresher. Two weeks later, Saskia still handles a surprise code-card drill. The burst has already gone soft.
examples.whatToDo: Trust the later drill, not the drama of the cram. Keep the weekly cycle because it makes the skill return after time and changed cues.
examples.whyItMatters: The burst can win the feeling of effort. The system wins when memory has to come back after the test room disappears.

examples.title: Thabo adds a repair ticket to the apprentice station

planSpec.audience: coaches building repair into recurring practice
planSpec.stakes: whether errors get revisited instead of repeated
planSpec.requiredBeat: he designs a repair loop for apprentice cooks

examples.scenario: Thabo clips a repair ticket above the garde-manger station at 2:37 p.m., tape snapping against the steel shelf. The apprentice cooks have practiced knife cuts, sauces, and plating in separate bursts. The same errors return on Fridays. The new ticket has three lines: what missed, when to retry, what changed. A crooked brunoise goes on the ticket before it goes in the compost. By dinner, the station has a memory.
examples.whatToDo: Make every recurring miss produce a repair ticket with a scheduled retry. Review the ticket during the next mixed prep block.
examples.whyItMatters: A system that finds errors but never revisits them stalls. The repair loop turns inspection into stronger next attempts.

examples.title: Inga moves the study tips onto Tuesday and Friday

planSpec.audience: readers collecting advice without scheduling it
planSpec.stakes: whether methods become a repeatable routine
planSpec.requiredBeat: she moves from tips to a calendar

examples.scenario: Inga opens a notes app at 9:14 p.m. on her apartment floor, laundry warm in a blue basket beside her. The list says retrieve, space, mix, check, repair, but for three weeks it has been only a list. She deletes the heading and creates two calendar blocks: Tuesday ten-minute recall, Friday mixed practice plus repair. The advice loses its shine when it becomes an alarm. It also becomes harder to ignore.
examples.whatToDo: Turn each method into a dated appointment with a small trigger and a clear finish line. Keep the routine short enough to survive a normal week.
examples.whyItMatters: Tips do not make learning stick until they ask for time. The calendar turns good ideas into repeated contact with memory.

questions.prompt: A student wants to use only flashcards for a final. What should be added?
choices: Spacing, mixed cases, checks, and repair so flashcards are part of a cycle
Only more colors on the cards
Nothing, because one tactic covers every weakness
questions.explanation: Flashcards help retrieval, but the full routine also handles forgetting, selection, calibration, and repair.

questions.prompt: Why is a calendar useful for learning?
choices: It guarantees motivation stays high
It makes methods recur after time and changed conditions
It removes the need for feedback
questions.explanation: A calendar gives retrieval, mixing, checking, and repair a return path. Inspiration alone often fades.

questions.prompt: Which routine best fits the synthesis?
choices: One long reread the night before
Only watching examples in order
Recall Tuesday, mixed practice Wednesday, no-cue check Thursday, repair Friday
questions.explanation: The routine combines the main moves and spreads them over time so memory has to return and improve.

questions.prompt: A training program checks errors but never revisits them. What is missing?
choices: A repair loop with another attempt
A prettier report
Less feedback
questions.explanation: Checking exposes weakness. Repair and retest strengthen it.

questions.prompt: What does interleaving add inside the full routine?
choices: A way to avoid retrieval
Practice choosing among related cases
A guarantee that practice feels smooth
questions.explanation: Interleaving trains selection. It complements retrieval and spacing by making learners choose the right move.

questions.prompt: A learner says the cram block felt more intense than the weekly plan. What evidence should decide?
choices: How dramatic the study felt
How late the learner stayed awake
Later performance after time and changed cues
questions.explanation: Durability is shown by later recall and use, not by the drama of the session.

questions.prompt: Design a small weekly cycle for a certification skill.
choices: Schedule recall, mixed cases, a no-cue check, and a repair round
Read every page once with no check
Wait until the final day
questions.explanation: A small cycle gives each method a job and keeps the skill returning across the week.

questions.prompt: Why can one strong tactic still fall short?
choices: Strong tactics never work
It may address one weakness while leaving others uncovered
Using a tactic means feedback is impossible
questions.explanation: Retrieval, spacing, mixing, calibration, and repair do different jobs. A single tool can leave gaps.

questions.prompt: What is the best final measure of a learning system?
choices: Whether the plan looks complex
Whether every session feels easy
Whether the skill returns and works under changed conditions
questions.explanation: A good system makes knowledge available later, with different cues and real use.

reviewCards.front: You have one favorite study tactic. What should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask what weakness it does not cover. Add spacing, mixing, checking, or repair so the tactic becomes part of a routine.

reviewCards.front: Why does repair belong in the system?
reviewCards.back: Because checks only reveal gaps. Repair schedules another attempt so the gap gets stronger instead of merely named.

reviewCards.front: What does the calendar add that advice lacks?
reviewCards.back: It makes the methods return. A scheduled recall or mixed practice block gives memory repeated work after time has passed.

reviewCards.front: How do the main moves reinforce each other?
reviewCards.back: Retrieval produces, spacing returns, interleaving chooses, calibration checks, and repair strengthens the miss. Together they cover more failure points than one method alone.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is building a repeatable learning cycle. Schedule retrieval, spacing, interleaving, calibration, and repair so the methods keep working after the first burst of motivation.

ifThenPlans.plan: If training advice lives only in a document, then schedule a recall check, a mixed case, and a repair round before the next deadline.
If a rehab or fitness cue keeps fading, then put two short return sessions on the calendar with one form check and one repair note.
If you collect study tips, then convert one tip into a dated recall block and one dated repair block this week.
If you are trying to improve a conversation habit, then schedule one recall of the cue, one live attempt, and one repair note afterward.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one skill and create a four-part calendar cycle: recall, mixed practice, no-cue check, and repair. Keep each block under fifteen minutes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Run the cycle for one week. At the end, ask what returned more easily, what still failed, and which repair block needs to repeat next week.

memorableLines.why: It makes routine design concrete and memorable.

memorableLines.why: It explains why synthesis matters without jargon.
